text: Chapter two: glass beads. And this time... you are Wren.
West Africa, five hundred years ago. On the Gold Coast, a rare blue bead, the accori, could be worth its weight in gold. All were old. Nobody made new ones.
Now you're a European trader. It's only glass, you think. I can make that! Europe's glassmakers tried. But people on the coast could tell the copies apart.

New plan: ordinary beads, by the ton. By the late seventeen hundreds, Venice made tens of millions a year. In Liverpool, the price of one ounce of gold bought nearly fifty kilos. Coastal merchants still bargained hard.
Ships carried them south, with cloth, iron and guns. They bought gold and ivory. Above all, Liverpool's traders bought people. Glass beads helped pay for the Atlantic slave trade.
Step off the ship. Imagine your family saved in ordinary beads: years of work, on a string. If every ship brings more beads, each one buys a little less. Same string. Less food.
Unless the string held an accori. Nobody could copy those. Two hundred years on, a Dutch trader wrote it still traded for its weight in gold.
Remember Ulm Hollow? Wren didn't steal. Wren just spent first, and pentaja savers paid the difference. When you're Wren, it feels like winning. Somebody always pays.
Next: North America, where shell beads became money... until metal drills arrived.
